title: Should you exercise early?
objectives: Show why exercising an American call on a stock with no dividends never pays.
Say when early exercise can pay: a call just before a large dividend, or a put deep in the money.

screens.prose: You hold an American call struck at £100.00, with a year to run. The share is at £130.00, pays no dividend, and the rate is 5%. Exercising now pays £30.00. You could sell the call instead.
screens.question: Using the bounds from l10, what is the least a buyer must pay for the call?

hints.text: The call's floor is $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$.
The strike, discounted a year at 5%, is £95.24.

feedback.correct: At least £34.76, more than the £30.00 that exercising pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the floor $S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$ with these numbers.

byKey.intrinsic: That is what exercising pays. The floor from l10 discounts the strike, so it is higher.
byKey.cap: That is the cap, the share price. The question asks for the least a buyer must pay.

explain.text: The floor is $130.00 - 95.24 = 34.76$, and a buyer who pays less hands you an arbitrage. So selling gets you at least £4.76 more than exercising. Exercising throws that money away.

screens.prose: The bold line is what exercising pays. The curve is what a model says the call is worth now, with a year left. Slide the share price across the whole range.
screens.question: Is there a share price where the call is worth less now than exercising would pay?

options.text: No: the curve stays above the line at every price
Yes, deep in the money, where the curve meets the line
options.why: You saw the curve close in on the line. Even at £150.00 it stays above it, by the interest on the strike.

options.text: Yes, at the strike, where the line has its kink
options.why: At the strike exercising pays 0, and the call is worth most above its payoff there.

feedback.correct: The curve is above the line everywhere: holding beats exercising.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the price to £150.00 and compare the curve with the line.

explain.text: Far above the strike the gap shrinks towards £4.76, the interest on £100.00. It never reaches 0. So an American call on a share with no dividend is never exercised early.

screens.prose: At £130.00 the model values the call at £35.33. Exercising pays £30.00. The gap is the call's **time value**, and it has two parts. One is interest: you pay the £100.00 a year later. The other is **insurance**: if the share falls below £100.00, you lose nothing more.
screens.question: How much of the £5.33 gap is interest on the strike?

hints.text: Paying £100.00 in a year costs how much today?
The floor sits £4.76 above the exercise value.

feedback.correct: £4.76 is interest; the other £0.57 is insurance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare £100.00 paid now with £100.00 paid in a year.

byKey.whole: That is the whole gap. Part of it is insurance, the value of not having to buy if the share falls.
byKey.insurance: That is the part left over, the insurance. Interest is the larger part here.
byKey.rate: You took 5% of £100.00 at the end of the year. Today that interest is worth $100.00 - 95.24 = 4.76$.

explain.text: Interest is $100.00 - 95.24 = 4.76$, the move from exercise value to floor. Insurance is $35.33 - 34.76 = 0.57$, small this deep in the money. Exercising early gives up both.

screens.prose: Slide the rate and watch the floor, $130.00 - 100.00/(1+r)$, move against the exercise value. Then set the rate to 0.
screens.question: At a rate of 0, should the holder of this American call exercise early?

options.text: No: the insurance part is still worth something, so selling still beats exercising
Yes: with no interest to earn there is no reason to wait
options.why: You counted only the interest part. Insurance remains: if the share falls below £100.00, the call holder loses less.

options.text: It makes no difference: the two are worth exactly the same
options.why: The floor meets the exercise value, but the call is worth more than its floor. A model gives £31.01 at a rate of 0.

hints.text: What happens to the floor at a rate of 0?
At $r = 0$ the floor meets the exercise value, £30.00.
The interest part is gone, but the insurance part is still above 0. Selling still wins, just by less.

feedback.correct: Still no. At $r = 0$ interest vanishes, but insurance does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which part of the time value survives at a rate of 0.

explain.text: At $r = 0$ the floor is $130.00 - 100.00 = 30.00$, the exercise value. The call is still worth more, about £31.01, for the insurance. A put is not exercised early at $r = 0$ either: waiting costs no interest.

screens.prose: Now the share pays a £5.00 dividend tomorrow, and three months remain. Tonight it is £130.00; tomorrow it opens near £125.00. Exercise tonight and you own the share, dividend included: £30.00. Wait, and a model values the call at £26.25 tomorrow.
screens.question: How much more does exercising tonight give than waiting?

hints.text: Compare the two points.
Exercise tonight is £30.00; waiting is £26.25.

feedback.correct: £3.75: here exercising just before the dividend pays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the value of waiting from the value of exercising tonight.

byKey.dividend: You took the whole dividend as the gain. Waiting keeps some value: interest on the strike and a little insurance.
byKey.sign: You have the sign reversed. Exercising tonight gives more than waiting.

explain.text: Only the share's owner gets the £5.00. Waiting saves interest on the strike for three months, about £1.21, plus a little insurance. The dividend outweighs both, so exercise just before the share goes ex-dividend.

screens.prose: Puts are different. You hold an American put struck at £100.00, with a year left, at 5%. The firm is near collapse: its share is £2.00. Exercising now pays £98.00. The most the put can ever pay is £100.00, if the share ends at 0.
screens.question: What is the best case, £100.00 in a year, worth today?

hints.text: Discount £100.00 for a year at 5%.
Compare the best case with £98.00 now.

feedback.correct: £95.24. Even the best case is worth less than exercising now.

byKey.undiscounted: You compared £100.00 in a year with £98.00 now. Money now earns interest: discount the £100.00.
byKey.grown: You grew £100.00 by a year's interest. To bring it back to today, divide by 1.05.

explain.text: Waiting can at best bring £100.00 in a year, worth £95.24 now. Exercising gives £98.00 today, which you can invest. Deep in the money, the interest on $K$ outweighs the little insurance left.

screens.prose: The curve is a model's value for a **European** put struck at £100.00, with a year left. The bold line is what exercising would pay. Slide the share price down from the strike.
screens.question: Below about which share price is the European put worth less than exercising would pay?

options.text: About £89.00
£100.00, the strike
options.why: At the strike exercising pays 0, and the put is worth more than that. The curve crosses the line lower down.

options.text: Never: an option is always worth at least its payoff
options.why: That is true for a call on a share with no dividend. Slide to £70.00: the put's curve is below the line.

options.text: About £50.00
options.why: You looked for the curve at its lowest. It crosses the line much nearer the strike.

hints.text: Find where the curve crosses the bold line.
Compare the two at £95.00 and at £85.00.
At £90.00 the curve is just above the line; at £88.00 it is below.

feedback.correct: Below about £89.00 the European put is worth less than its exercise value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to where the curve and the bold line cross.

explain.text: Below about £89.31 the curve sits under the line, by up to the interest on $K$. A European holder must wait, but an American holder exercises there. The trees course finds that boundary on a tree in l7.

screens.prose: A colleague holds the American call from the start: struck at £100.00, share at £130.00, a year left, no dividend. She fears a fall and wants to exercise to lock in her £30.00 gain.
screens.question: What is her best way to lock in the gain?

options.text: Sell the call, which gets at least £34.76
Exercise: a gain in hand is safe
options.why: You locked in £30.00 and left at least £4.76 behind. Selling banks more, just as safely.

options.text: Hold: the share may rise further
options.why: Holding keeps her exposed to the fall she fears. Selling locks in the value now.

options.text: Exercise: deep in-the-money puts are exercised early, so calls are too
options.why: You carried the put rule over to calls. A put's holder gets $K$ early; a call's holder pays $K$ early, which only costs interest.

hints.text: What do the two choices pay today?
Selling gets at least the floor, £34.76.
Exercise pays £30.00 and selling at least £34.76. Both end her exposure; one pays more.

feedback.correct: Sell. Both end her exposure, and selling pays more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what exercising and selling each bring today.

byKey.exercise: You chose to lock in by exercising. Selling locks in too, and pays at least £4.76 more.
byKey.put-rule: You applied the put rule to a call. For a call, early exercise pays the strike early, which only costs interest.

explain.text: Exercising pays £30.00; selling pays at least £34.76. If she cannot sell, she can short one share against the call, which also locks in the gain. Exercising early is never the best way out.

screens.prose: We showed it with numbers. Now the general case: write $C$ for an American call and $c$ for the European call with the same strike and expiry, on a share with no dividend, with $r > 0$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $C \ge c$: the American call has every right the European one has, and more
$c \ge S_0 - K/(1+r)^T$, the floor from l10
So $C > S_0 - K$: selling beats exercising, and $C = c$

hints.text: Start from what exercising pays.
Chain the American call down to the European floor, then compare floors.
Exercise value, $C \ge c$, the floor, then compare $K/(1+r)^T$ with $K$, then conclude.

feedback.correct: A chain of inequalities from the American call down to its exercise value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound $C$ below by $c$, $c$ by its floor, then compare the floor with $S_0 - K$.

byKey.d: Comparing the floor with $S_0 - K$ needs the floor first. Put the l10 line above it.
byKey.e: The conclusion needs every inequality above it.

explain.text: Each line is a bound, so the chain gives $C > S_0 - K$ whenever $r > 0$. The early-exercise right is then worth nothing, so $C = c$. A dividend breaks line 3, which is why the dividend case can differ.

screens.prose: You hold employee share options: American calls struck at £20.00 on your firm's share, now £45.00, expiring in four years. The firm pays no dividend. The rules forbid selling or hedging the options.
screens.question: What does this lesson say about exercising now?

options.text: Selling would beat exercising, but you cannot sell, so exercising early to spread your risk can make sense
Never exercise early: the rule holds whatever the rules allow
options.why: The rule compares exercising with selling. If you cannot sell or hedge, that comparison is not open to you.

options.text: Exercise now: £25.00 a share in hand beats waiting
options.why: Exercising gives up the time value, at least £3.55 a share here. It is a cost you pay for cashing out.

options.text: Exercise only once the share stops rising
options.why: No one knows when a share stops rising. The decision is about time value against your need to cash out.

hints.text: The no-early-exercise rule assumes you can sell. Can you?
If sellable, the option would be worth at least £28.55 a share.
You cannot sell, so the choice is to hold, or exercise and sell the shares to diversify.

feedback.correct: The rule is about selling against exercising. Without a sale, early exercise trades time value for safety.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the rule assumes you can do.

explain.text: With $K/(1+r)^T$ at 5% for four years, the floor is $45.00 - 20.00/1.05^4 = 28.55$. Employees often exercise early anyway, to cut their exposure to one firm. Taxes on exercise and on the share sale differ by country and can tip the timing either way.

screens.prose: A desk prices one-year puts struck at £100.00, at 5% and 20% volatility, with a 1,000-step tree. The American put can be exercised early; the European one cannot. The difference is the **early-exercise premium**.
screens.question: Fill in the early-exercise premium at each share price.

hints.text: The premium is American less European.
At £80.00 the American put is worth exactly its exercise value, £20.00.

feedback.correct: 2.92, 1.24, 0.51, 0.19 and 0.07: the deeper in the money, the larger the premium.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the European price from the American price in each row.

explain.text: The premium grows as the put goes deeper in the money, where early exercise is most likely. At £80.00 the American put is worth $100.00 - 80.00$: exercise at once. Far out of the money the right is almost never used, so it is worth little.

ideas: Exercising a call early pays the strike sooner and throws away the insurance. On a share with no dividend, selling always beats exercising, so $C = c$.
A large dividend can make exercising a call just before the ex-date pay: only the share's owner collects it.
Deep in the money, an American put is worth exercising early: the interest on $K$ received now outweighs what is left of the insurance.

formula.name: No early exercise of a call
formula.note: Needs $r > 0$ and no dividend before expiry. At $r = 0$ the last step is an equality, and insurance still makes holding win.

summary.trap: Exercising a call to lock in a gain leaves money behind: selling it, or shorting the share, locks in more. Puts do not follow the call rule.

quiz.prose: An American call struck at £50.00 has two years to run. The share is at £70.00 and pays no dividend. The rate is 4% a year.
quiz.question: How much more than exercising must selling the call fetch, at the least?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The extra is $K - K/(1+r)^T$.

byKey.simple: You took 4% of £50.00 for two years. Discounting gives $50.00 - 50.00/1.04^2 = 3.77$.
byKey.one-year: You discounted for one year. The call has two years to run.

explain.text: Exercise pays $70.00 - 50.00 = 20.00$. The floor is $70.00 - 50.00/1.04^2 = 70.00 - 46.23 = 23.77$. Selling fetches at least £3.77 more.

quiz.prose: Four American options, each well in the money.
quiz.question: Which one might its holder rationally exercise early?

options.text: A put on a share that has collapsed close to 0
A call on a share with no dividend that has doubled
options.why: You thought a big gain should be cashed. On a share with no dividend, selling the call always beats exercising.

options.text: A call on a share with no dividend, when rates are 0
options.why: At a rate of 0 the interest part vanishes, but insurance still makes the call worth more than its exercise value.

options.text: A put deep in the money, when rates are 0 and there are no dividends
options.why: At a rate of 0, getting $K$ early earns nothing, so waiting costs nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Early exercise pays only when receiving cash now earns more than the right to wait.

explain.text: Exercising the put pays almost $K$ now, and $K$ now earns interest. Waiting adds almost nothing: the share cannot fall much below 0. With rates at 0 neither option is exercised early.

quiz.prose: An American call struck at £80.00 is deep in the money, with the share at £120.00 and one month left. Tomorrow the share goes ex-dividend, paying £6.00. Waiting saves about 30p of interest on the strike, and the insurance is worth about 5p.
quiz.question: What should the holder do tonight?

options.text: Exercise tonight, to collect the £6.00 dividend
Sell: an American call is never exercised early
options.why: That rule needs no dividends. Here the £6.00 dwarfs the 35p of time value.

options.text: Wait until expiry, to keep the insurance
options.why: The insurance is worth about 5p, the dividend £6.00.

options.text: Nothing: the call's price already includes the dividend
options.why: The holder of the call never receives the dividend. Only the share's owner does.

feedback.correct: Exercise tonight: £6.00 of dividend against about 35p of time value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what waiting saves with what the dividend pays.

explain.text: Exercising tonight makes you the owner when the dividend is paid. Waiting saves about $0.30 + 0.05 = 0.35$. The dividend is worth far more, so exercise just before the ex-date.
